summary: Teaches biodiversity (the variety of different species in an ecosystem) and keystone species (those whose impact far exceeds their abundance or size) to ages 9\u201311. Core goal: learners trace trophic cascades through a food web, distinguish variety from sheer numbers, and connect biodiversity to resilience and ecosystem services. A proposed core approach has learners perturb a food web (remove/restore a species) and follow the ripple across levels; supporting activities include a prediction-based case study of the Yellowstone wolves, ordering/matching to catch key misconceptions, and discussion of why a small species can hold a whole system together. These are research-informed proposals, not validated or required interaction designs.
misconceptions: 'Biodiversity just means lots of animals' — it means a variety of different species, not a large number of individuals.
'Every species matters equally / removing one animal barely changes anything' — keystone species have disproportionate effects and their loss can cascade.
'The biggest or most numerous animal is always the most important' — keystone species can be small or few (sea otters, bees).
'Ecosystems bounce back easily from any loss' — losing a keystone species can permanently reshape an ecosystem.
'A trophic cascade only goes one step' — effects ripple through multiple levels of the food web (and even to physical features like rivers).

activities.title: Perturb a food web: remove a species and follow the ripple
steps: Start from a connected food web (e.g. Yellowstone: wolves, elk, willow/aspen, beavers, songbirds, riverbanks) with a visible population indicator for each species.
Predict in writing what will happen to elk, to willow and aspen, and to beavers/birds if the wolves are removed \u2014 before changing anything.

Remove the wolves and observe the chain: the elk that wolves had kept in check increase, willows get grazed to almost nothing, beavers and songbirds that depended on the willows decline, and riverbanks become less stable as bank vegetation is lost.

Restore the wolves and watch the system partially knit back together \u2014 fewer/warier elk, willows regrow, beavers return, banks steady \u2014 noting that recovery can be partial and slow, and some changes may not fully reverse.
Repeat removing a minor, weakly connected species and compare how small the ripple is.
Write one sentence explaining what made the wolves' removal cause a far bigger cascade than removing the minor species.
activities.insight: Some species are keystones: their impact on the whole system is disproportionate to their size or numbers, because of the strong role they play (for example, controlling a plant-eater that would otherwise overgraze). Removing one keystone ripples through multiple levels of the food web and can even reshape physical features like rivers. Recovery after restoring a keystone can be incomplete or slow \u2014 ecosystems do not always bounce back easily from a keystone loss.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: the Yellowstone wolves
steps: Read/hear the case: wolves were removed from Yellowstone for decades, then reintroduced.
Before any reveal, predict with reasons what happened to the elk, to the willow and aspen, and to the rivers.

Compare predictions with what scientists have reported: elk heavily browsed willow and aspen while wolves were gone; after wolves returned (alongside other changes such as elk hunting, more bears and cougars, and drought), willow and aspen recovered in some places, beaver colonies increased (helped by beavers released near the park), and some stream banks may be steadier \u2014 though recovery is patchy and scientists still debate how much was caused by wolves.
Discuss why a one-step prediction like 'more elk' misses the far-reaching effects.
activities.insight: Effects of losing or restoring a keystone species ripple through many levels, surprising a naive 'one-step' prediction. Interdependence means a single change can reshape an ecosystem.

activities.title: Biodiversity vs. abundance, and why variety means resilience
steps: Compare two ponds/fields: one with a million individuals of a single species, one with many different species. Decide which has higher biodiversity and justify it.
Compare a species-rich food web with a species-poor one. In each, remove one link and describe what happens.

Explain why the rich web often copes better with a loss (other species can fill similar roles \u2014 'backups'), while the sparse web is more likely to collapse \u2014 though even a rich web can change greatly if the lost species is a keystone with no backup.
Name at least two ecosystem services that biodiversity supports (e.g. pollination, clean water, food).
activities.insight: Biodiversity is the variety of different species, not the number of individuals. Greater variety is associated with greater stability and resilience and underpins services people rely on.

activities.title: Order the cascade and match keystones to their roles
steps: Put the steps of a cascade in order, e.g. sea otters \u2192 urchins \u2192 kelp \u2192 many kelp-forest species (otters removed \u2192 urchins explode \u2192 kelp grazed down \u2192 dependent species decline).

Match keystone species to the role that makes them keystones: sea otters (control urchins that would destroy kelp forests), wolves (limit and move elk, which can help vegetation recover in places), bees (pollination).
Answer: a pond with a million fish all of one kind \u2014 is that high biodiversity? Explain.
Answer: is removing a predator always good for the animals it used to eat? Explain using overgrazing/overpopulation.
activities.insight: Keystone status comes from a species' role in the web, not from its size or numbers; cascades run through several linked steps; removing a predator can harm the whole system via overpopulation.

activities.title: Discussion: how can something small hold a whole ecosystem together?
steps: Discuss the hook question: 'Why did bringing back one predator change a whole park?' or 'The sea otter isn't big \u2014 how can it be a keystone for the whole kelp forest?'
Explain in your own words that a keystone's importance is about its role and connections, not its size.
Give a new example or scenario and predict what losing that species might cause.
activities.insight: Importance in an ecosystem is about role and connectedness, not size or numbers \u2014 a felt answer to a counterintuitive question.

checkQuestion: In some seas, hunters removed nearly all the sea otters. Sea otters aren't the biggest animal there, so a student predicts 'removing them won't change much.' What actually happens to the kelp forest when the otters are gone — and why?
checkAnswer: Removing the otters sets off a chain reaction (a trophic cascade). Otters eat sea urchins; with the otters gone, urchin numbers explode and the urchins graze the kelp forest down until it disappears. That kelp forest was home and food for many other species, so they decline too. The sea otter is a keystone species — not because it's big, but because its role holds the whole ecosystem together — so losing it changes far more than one species.
